title: Gastrointestinal Comprehensive Set 1: GI Motility (Short Answer)

questions.prompt: Identify the specific cells located in the myenteric plexus that serve as the pacemakers for gastrointestinal smooth muscle electrical activity.
questions.modelAnswer: Interstitial cells of Cajal.

questions.prompt: Define "slow waves" in the context of gastrointestinal smooth muscle and clarify if they are considered action potentials.
questions.modelAnswer: They are oscillating membrane potentials (depolarization/repolarization), not action potentials, though they determine the pattern of action potentials.

questions.prompt: Which specific ion channel opening is responsible for the depolarising phase of a slow wave?
questions.modelAnswer: Calcium (Ca^(2+)) channels.

questions.prompt: Which specific ion movement is responsible for the repolarising phase of a slow wave?
questions.modelAnswer: Outward potassium (K^+) current.

questions.prompt: State the characteristic frequency of slow waves in the stomach versus the duodenum.
questions.modelAnswer: Stomach: 3 per minute; Duodenum: 12 per minute.

questions.prompt: Although slow waves are not action potentials, what is their relationship to the threshold potential and subsequent muscle contraction?
questions.modelAnswer: Slow waves bring the membrane potential toward threshold; if threshold is reached, action potentials occur on the peak of the slow wave, triggering contraction.

questions.prompt: How does the number of action potentials occurring at the peak of a slow wave correlate with the resulting muscle tension?
questions.modelAnswer: The greater the number of action potentials, the higher the tension/force of the phasic contraction.

questions.prompt: Explain the "all-or-none" property as it applies to GI action potentials.
questions.modelAnswer: If a stimulus is at or above threshold, the action potential occurs with a constant amplitude and form; it will not occur if the stimulus is subthreshold.

questions.prompt: Name the three phases of the swallowing reflex and specify which are voluntary and which are involuntary.
questions.modelAnswer: Oral (voluntary), pharyngeal (involuntary), and esophageal (involuntary).

questions.prompt: Where is the swallowing center located in the brainstem?
questions.modelAnswer: Medulla (and lower pons).

questions.prompt: Describe the protective mechanisms that prevent food from entering the nasopharynx and trachea during the pharyngeal phase of swallowing.
questions.modelAnswer: Nasopharynx: Soft palate is pulled upward. Trachea: Epiglottis covers the larynx, and the larynx moves upward.

questions.prompt: Contrast primary esophageal peristalsis with secondary esophageal peristalsis regarding their triggers.
questions.modelAnswer: Primary: Triggered by the swallowing reflex. Secondary: Triggered by distension of the esophagus by remaining food.

questions.prompt: Which neurotransmitter, released by postganglionic peptidergic vagal fibers, is primarily responsible for the relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES)?
questions.modelAnswer: Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP).

questions.prompt: Explain the "receptive relaxation" (accommodation) reflex of the orad stomach and name the vagal neurotransmitter involved.
questions.modelAnswer: A vagovagal reflex that allows the orad stomach to expand to accommodate food without a large pressure increase; mediated by VIP.

questions.prompt: Contrast the primary motor functions of the orad region versus the caudad region of the stomach.
questions.modelAnswer: Orad: Receiving and storage (reservoir). Caudad: Mixing, digestion (trituration), and propulsion.

questions.prompt: Describe the process of "retropulsion" in the gastric antrum and its functional significance for digestion.
questions.modelAnswer: The propulsion of chyme back into the stomach when the wave of contraction closes the pylorus; it facilitates mixing and particle size reduction.

questions.prompt: What are the "migrating myoelectric complexes" (MMC), and how frequently do they occur during the interdigestive state?
questions.modelAnswer: Periodic contractions/peristaltic waves that clear the gut of residue; they occur every 90 minutes.

questions.prompt: Which hormone is the primary mediator for initiating MMCs?
questions.modelAnswer: Motilin.

questions.prompt: How do liquids, solids, and non-isotonic chyme differ in their rates of gastric emptying?
questions.modelAnswer: Liquids empty fastest; solids empty slower (must be reduced to <1mm³); isotonic contents empty faster than hypertonic or hypotonic contents.

questions.prompt: Which duodenal hormone, released in response to fat, acts to slow gastric emptying?
questions.modelAnswer: Cholecystokinin (CCK).

questions.prompt: Explain how low pH in the duodenum inhibits gastric emptying.
questions.modelAnswer: Mediated by enteric nervous system reflexes; H^+ receptors in the duodenum detect low pH and slow emptying to allow for neutralization by pancreatic bicarbonate.

questions.prompt: Contrast the mechanical goals of segmentation contractions versus peristaltic contractions in the small intestine.
questions.modelAnswer: Segmentation: Mixing chyme and exposing it to enzymes/mucosa. Peristalsis: Propelling chyme along the tract.

questions.prompt: In the peristaltic reflex of the small intestine, what is the coordinated response of the circular and longitudinal muscles behind (orad to) the food bolus?
questions.modelAnswer: Circular muscle contracts; longitudinal muscle relaxes.

questions.prompt: In the peristaltic reflex, what is the coordinated response of the circular and longitudinal muscles in front of (caudad to) the food bolus?
questions.modelAnswer: Circular muscle relaxes; longitudinal muscle contracts.

questions.prompt: Which substance, released by mucosal enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells, initiates the peristaltic reflex by binding to receptors on intrinsic primary afferent neurons (IPANs)?
questions.modelAnswer: Serotonin (5-HT).

questions.prompt: What are the characteristic saclike segments formed by contractions of the large intestine called?
questions.modelAnswer: Haustra.

questions.prompt: Define "mass movements" in the colon and state how often they typically occur.
questions.modelAnswer: Powerful contractile waves that move contents over long distances; 1 to 3 times per day.

questions.prompt: Explain the "gastrocolic reflex" and identify the hormones that mediate its efferent limb.
questions.modelAnswer: Food in the stomach increases colonic motility/mass movements; mediated by CCK and gastrin.

questions.prompt: Describe the "rectosphincteric reflex" triggered by the filling of the rectum.
questions.modelAnswer: Rectal distension causing the rectal wall to contract and the internal anal sphincter to relax.

questions.prompt: Contrast the muscle types and innervation of the internal versus the external anal sphincters.
questions.modelAnswer: Internal: Unitary smooth muscle (involuntary); External: Striated muscle (voluntary).

questions.prompt: Identify the clinical condition caused by a congenital absence of the myenteric plexus in the distal colon, resulting in severe constipation.
questions.modelAnswer: Megacolon (Hirschsprung's disease).
